# I had an AI build a construction schedule: a scheduling component made for transportation worked unchanged on a construction site (build log #174)

> **Build log series**: I hand my own design system `@gunjo/ui` ([Gunjo](https://gunjo.jp)) to an AI that has never seen it, and have it build real screens. This time I am expanding into construction. The brief: a **construction schedule screen for a site supervisor**. It brings together schedule bars for each type of work, progress and work completed, the contractor in charge, milestones, weather, and site operations.

## Result: 4/5. The scheduling component worked unchanged across industries

I gave an AI that had never seen Gunjo nothing but the public npm package and the gunjo.jp docs, and asked it to build the screen. `tsc` passed clean, and the screen works on both mobile and desktop.

The highlight is that **the `Gantt` scheduling component fit a construction schedule with almost no changes, even though it was not built for construction**. This `Gantt` was originally added to Gunjo for aircraft operating rotations and production-line resource planning. Its rows and time axis, the line marking today, the interaction for selecting a bar and opening its details, and even its screen reader labels all worked unchanged for a schedule of construction work.

The existing components also fit naturally outside the schedule itself.

- **`Timeline`**: it worked unchanged for milestones such as interim inspections, framing completion, and handover.
- **`Meter`**: its options for showing overall work completed against a target (`target` and the "higher is better" direction) matched the meaning of construction progress exactly.
- **`DataTable`**: row clicks open details, and small meters can sit inside cells, so it covered both the list of work types and the detail view.
- **`StatGroup`**: it could correctly reverse the color meaning for a metric where an increase is bad, such as the number of delays.

The same UI components can be reused even when the industry changes. This round confirmed that in construction as well.

## What was missing: dependency lines and progress inside the schedule bars

At the same time, two construction-specific requirements exposed clear gaps in Gunjo. Both are missing features in the scheduling component.

1. **There is no way to connect predecessor and successor work with lines.** I wanted to draw dependencies such as "the frame starts after the foundation is complete" as arrows between the schedule bars, but `Gantt` does not have that feature. This time I fell back to listing the preceding work as text in the detail panel. Dependencies are one of the most important parts of a construction schedule, so this is the largest gap.
2. **There is no way to fill a bar to show progress (work completed).** I wanted each bar to show how far that type of work had progressed, but this is not available as a standard feature either. This time I borrowed a mechanism intended for another purpose as a substitute.

I also had to hand-roll part of the color legend and the loading skeleton because the existing components could not cover them completely. The hand-rolled portion was about 80 lines out of roughly 870 for the whole screen, so it was only a small part. Most of the screen came together by composing existing components.

I follow the rule of three: a missing component gets built for real and added to Gunjo only after three separate screens have needed it independently. This is only the first appearance for the dependency lines and progress inside bars.

## Where the names got confusing

The scheduling components have similar names, which made the choice unclear. `ScheduleGrid` looks like the leading candidate from its name alone, but it is a timetable organized by period and day of the week, not a project schedule. `Gantt` was the right component. The names were not enough to decide, and the purpose became clear only after reading each description. There is room to make the entry point for finding components by use case more prominent.

## Wrapping up

Construction is far removed from the foundational UI and finance screens Gunjo has covered before. Even so, the skeleton of the screen, the schedule, progress, list and details, and milestones, came together unchanged from components built for other industries. The only parts left uncovered were two construction-specific needs: dependency lines and progress inside schedule bars. As I add more industries, the components that work in common and the gaps that appear only in a particular industry separate more clearly.
